title: Compute Systems: VMs, GKE, Serverless, VMware Engine, and Orchestration
bodyMarkdown:
## Pick the operating model, then the pricing model, then the automation

Compute questions have three layers: how much of the stack Google runs (VM, Kubernetes, container, function, VMware), how you pay and what capacity assurance you need, and how you keep the fleet reproducible and patched. The exam rewards the least operationally heavy option that still meets every stated constraint.

## The compute spectrum

| Option | You manage | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|
| Compute Engine | Guest OS and everything above | Full OS control, custom kernels, licensed software, GPUs and TPUs, lift-and-shift |
| [Google Cloud VMware Engine](https://cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/overview) | VMware workloads; Google runs the stack | Keep vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX and HCX tooling and skills unchanged |
| GKE Standard | Node pools, scaling, capacity | Privileged Pods, DaemonSets with host access, specific node shapes |
| GKE Autopilot | Workloads only; billed per Pod requests | Production Kubernetes with minimal operations |
| Cloud Run | Container or source only | Stateless HTTP services, jobs, scale to zero |

### VMware Engine versus Migrate to Virtual Machines

VMware Engine runs your VMware environment on **dedicated bare-metal nodes** in Google Cloud, with Google handling upgrades, backups and health monitoring. The stack stays the same, so it is the lowest-change lift-and-shift. [Migrate to Virtual Machines](https://cloud.google.com/migrate/virtual-machines/docs/5.0/concepts/overview) instead moves VMs and disks from vSphere, AWS or Azure into native Compute Engine VMs. Rule: "keep vCenter, vSAN and NSX unchanged" means VMware Engine; "convert to Compute Engine instances" means Migrate to Virtual Machines.

## Machine families and custom machine types

Choose the [machine family](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/machine-resource) by workload shape:

| Family | Example series | Choose it for |
|---|---|---|
| General-purpose | N4, N2, E2, T2D | Web, microservices, business apps, dev and test |
| Compute-optimized | C4, C3, H3 | HPC, simulation, demanding web servers |
| Memory-optimized | M4, M3, X4 | In-memory databases; up to 12 TB of memory |
| Storage-optimized | Z3, Z4D | High storage density: SQL and NoSQL databases, search |
| Accelerator-optimized | A4, A3, G2 | CUDA workloads: ML training, inference, HPC |

[Custom machine types](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/creating-instance-with-custom-machine-type) exist for the N-series, E2 and G2. Memory is 2 to 8 GB per vCPU in 256 MiB steps (E2 allows 2 to 32 vCPUs), and they cost slightly more than the equivalent predefined type. Extended memory goes beyond 8 GB per vCPU on N-series but not E2, and does not qualify for committed use discounts. Use custom types when no predefined shape fits.

## Pricing and capacity models

Price and capacity are separate questions: a discount lowers cost, while only a reservation (or a scheduler that waits for hardware) addresses availability.

| Model | Discount and terms | Capacity assurance | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| On-demand | None | None | Unpredictable or short-lived load |
| [Spot VMs](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot) | Up to 91% off; price changes daily | None; preemptible, no SLA | Fault-tolerant, checkpointed batch |
| [Committed use discounts](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/committed-use-discounts-overview) | 1 or 3 years; resource-based or spend-based | None | Steady always-on baselines |
| [On-demand reservations](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/reservations-overview) | On-demand rate while they exist; combinable with commitments | Yes, within minutes | Capacity now, any duration |
| [Future reservations](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/future-reservations-overview) | On-demand reservation rate once provisioned | Yes, on a future date, after approval | Known events, migrations, scarce GPUs |
| [Flex-start VMs](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/provisioning-models) | Up to 53% off on A4, A3, A2, G4 and TPU | Best effort; provisioned when available | Short GPU or TPU jobs |
| [Sole-tenant nodes](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/nodes/sole-tenant-nodes) | Billed per full node | Dedicated hardware | BYOL or compliance |

**Spot VMs** replaced preemptible VMs and have **no maximum runtime**, but they do not auto-restart, do not live migrate, and carry no SLA. On preemption you get a best-effort shutdown of up to 30 seconds (the notice period is configurable as 120 seconds or 0, default 0), then `STOP` (default; disks still bill) or `DELETE`. A **managed instance group** recreates preempted instances. Pair Spot with checkpointing.

**Committed use discounts.** Resource-based CUDs commit to vCPUs, memory, GPUs or Local SSD in one region and project, with discounts up to 55% (up to 70% for memory-optimized), and **cannot be cancelled**. **Compute flexible CUDs** commit to hourly spend across Compute Engine, GKE and Cloud Run in a billing account, at roughly 17 to 63% depending on series and term. **Neither type guarantees capacity.** A resource-based commitment can be bought with attached reservations to get both.

**Sole-tenant nodes** are physical servers dedicated to your project, for per-core BYOL licensing and compliance isolation. You create a node template, then a node group in a zone, then place VMs on it.

### Planning scarce capacity: reservations, future reservations, Flex-start

Quota, price and commitments do not guarantee GPU or TPU capacity. Pick the lever by when you need it and for how long.

- **On-demand reservation.** Verifies availability and holds resources within minutes; keep it as long as you like and consume, modify or delete it any time. You pay the on-demand rate **whether or not VMs use it**, so set auto-delete for time-boxed needs. A VM consumes it only if project, zone, machine type, GPU and Local SSD configuration, and affinity match.
- **Future reservation.** A request for capacity starting on a date up to **one year ahead**, for at least **24 hours**. Google Cloud reviews it and approves or declines; a declined request can be edited and resubmitted. You pay nothing until resources provision, and the request locks 56 days before its start, after which it cannot be cancelled. Choose it for a migration, a peak sales event, or hard-to-get hardware.
- **Future reservation in calendar mode.** GPU, H4D or TPU capacity for **24 hours to 90 days**, approved within about a minute, with no quota needed for GPU or TPU. Auto-delete is mandatory and only VMs targeting the reservation can consume it. Beyond 90 days, capacity blocks arranged through your account team fit long pre-training.
- **Flex-start VMs** (Dynamic Workload Scheduler). No assurance of a start time: the request waits for hardware (up to two hours for a standalone VM; a MIG keeps retrying until resources appear), then runs for **up to seven days**. Supported shapes are limited (A4, A3, A2, G4, G2, some TPUs, N1 with GPUs, H4D). Choose it for fine-tuning and batch inference.

**Decision shorthand.** Steady baseline, no interruption: CUD. Interruptible batch: Spot in a MIG. Capacity now: on-demand reservation. Capacity on a known date: future reservation. Time-boxed GPU or TPU run under 90 days: calendar mode. Short run, flexible start: Flex-start. Licensing or isolation mandate: sole-tenant.

## GKE: Autopilot versus Standard

The [cluster mode guide](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/choose-cluster-mode) calls Autopilot the **recommended** mode. GKE manages nodes, bin-packing and scaling, applies security best practices by default, and you pay for the resources your **Pods request**. Standard gives you node-pool control, you pay per node, and you plan capacity. Autopilot prevents privileged Pods by default, so privileged or custom-node workloads belong on Standard.

Networking: [VPC-native clusters](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips) (alias IP ranges) are the default. Pods use a secondary range, with each node allocated a `/24` supporting up to 110 Pods per node in Standard and 32 in Autopilot. When ranges run out you can create a new cluster, lower max Pods per node, or add discontiguous multi-Pod CIDR ranges, so plan Pod ranges before creation.

**Private clusters.** [Private nodes](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/private-cluster-concept) have only internal IPs and need Cloud NAT to reach the internet. Control plane access is separate: a **private endpoint** reachable only from the VPC, or a public endpoint restricted by **authorized networks** (up to 100 IPv4 ranges). The recommended path is the DNS-based endpoint, which uses IAM instead of IP lists.

**Ingress traffic.** Use the [Gateway API](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/gateway-api): platform teams own `Gateway` objects, app teams own `HTTPRoute`s, and the `GatewayClass` picks the load balancer. Gateway is the recommended successor to Ingress.

## Cloud Run and serverless networking

[Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) offers **services** (autoscaled HTTP handling), **jobs** (run-to-completion tasks) and **worker pools** (pull-based background work); functions deploy onto the same platform. Services scale to zero unless you set minimum instances. Billing is **request-based** (pay only while handling requests) or **instance-based**.

To reach private VPC resources, use [Direct VPC egress](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/vpc-direct-vpc) or a Serverless VPC Access connector. Direct VPC places instances on your subnet, avoiding connector costs and latency. Cloud Run reserves IPs in blocks of 16 (`/28`), so subnets should be `/26` or larger.

### Event-driven triggers with Eventarc

[Eventarc](https://cloud.google.com/eventarc/docs/overview) is a fully managed service that routes events from sources to targets in CloudEvents format, so a Cloud Run service reacts to Google Cloud changes without polling.

| Edition | Model | Limits and targets |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | Triggers filter events from a provider to one destination | 512 KB events; 500 triggers per project per region; Cloud Run, GKE, Workflows |
| Advanced | Bus and pipelines, with CEL transformation and cross-project delivery | 1 MB events; one bus and 100 pipelines per project; adds Cloud Run jobs |

Sources are Google providers, as **direct events** (for example `google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized` when an object lands) or **Cloud Audit Logs** entries, plus third-party providers on Standard. Direct events arrive in seconds; audit-log events take under a minute and need the matching audit logs enabled. The trigger's service account needs `roles/eventarc.eventReceiver` plus `roles/run.invoker` on the target service.

Delivery is **at least once with no ordering guarantee**. The router POSTs to the service; a `2xx` response acknowledges it and anything else is retried with exponential backoff, with 24-hour default retention. Handlers must therefore be **idempotent**. Choose Eventarc to react to Google Cloud events; use Pub/Sub directly for your own publishers and fan-out, and Workflows for multi-step orchestration.

## Data processing and batch compute

Pick the engine by code and ops model, not data size:

| Service | Model | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|
| [Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/overview) | Serverless Apache Beam for batch and streaming; autoscaling | New unified streaming or batch ETL, no cluster to run |
| [Dataproc](https://cloud.google.com/dataproc/docs/concepts/overview) | Managed Spark, Hadoop, Hive and Pig, or serverless Spark | Migrating existing Spark or Hadoop jobs |
| [Batch](https://cloud.google.com/batch/docs/get-started) | Managed job scheduler on Compute Engine VMs, optional GPUs | Containerized or script jobs and HPC-style task arrays |

Run Dataproc as **ephemeral, job-scoped clusters** (they start in about 90 seconds) with data in Cloud Storage or BigQuery.

## Infrastructure orchestration and patching

- **[Infrastructure Manager](https://cloud.google.com/infrastructure-manager/docs/overview)** deploys Terraform as a managed service: state in Cloud Storage, runs in an ephemeral Cloud Build environment, revisions tracked, previews available.
- **[Config Connector](https://cloud.google.com/config-connector/docs/overview)** is a Kubernetes add-on whose CRDs manage Google Cloud resources declaratively. Config Controller is the managed variant.
- **[VM Manager](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/vm-manager)** provides patch management (on-demand or scheduled), OS inventory, and OS policies. It needs the OS Config agent and is paid.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Spot VMs for the always-on baseline.** Interruption and no SLA break the requirement; use CUDs.
- **Expecting a CUD to guarantee capacity.** It does not; add a reservation.
- **A reservation left running after the event.** It bills until deleted; use auto-delete.
- **Waiting for Flex-start on a fixed launch date.** It starts only when hardware is available; use a future reservation.
- **Resource-based CUDs for a shifting estate.** They cannot be cancelled; flexible CUDs fit.
- **VMware Engine when you want native VMs.** That is Migrate to Virtual Machines.
- **Polling a bucket on a schedule, or assuming exactly-once, ordered events.** Use an Eventarc trigger and idempotent handlers.
- **Always-on Hadoop cluster for periodic jobs.** Use ephemeral Dataproc clusters.
- **Hand-patching VMs and console-built infrastructure.** Use VM Manager and Infrastructure Manager.

## Exam tips

- **Stateless container, spiky, scale to zero:** Cloud Run.
- **Hands-off Kubernetes billed per Pod request:** GKE Autopilot; privileged or node-specific needs: Standard.
- **Unchanged vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX:** VMware Engine. Convert VMs to Compute Engine: Migrate to Virtual Machines.
- **Steady, uninterrupted baseline:** committed use discounts. Interruptible and checkpointed: Spot VMs in a managed instance group.
- **Guaranteed capacity requires a reservation.** CUDs give a discount, not capacity; Spot VMs have no SLA, no max runtime and a 30-second best-effort shutdown.
- **Capacity on a future date or for scarce GPUs:** future reservation (up to a year ahead, minimum 24 hours); GPU or TPU for up to 90 days: calendar mode.
- **Flex-start VMs (Dynamic Workload Scheduler) run up to 7 days but start only when hardware is available.** They are not a capacity guarantee.
- **React to a Cloud Storage upload or audit-log event with Cloud Run:** Eventarc trigger. Delivery is at least once and unordered, so make the handler idempotent.
- **Serverless stream or batch ETL means Dataflow;** existing Spark or Hadoop code means Dataproc; queued VM-based jobs and task arrays mean Batch.
- **Custom machine types fit odd CPU-to-memory ratios** (2 to 8 GB per vCPU).
- **Private GKE:** private nodes need Cloud NAT; restrict the control plane with authorized networks or a private or DNS endpoint.
- **Terraform as a managed service means Infrastructure Manager;** Kubernetes-native resource management means Config Connector; OS patching means VM Manager.
- **Serverless reaching private resources:** Direct VPC egress (preferred) or a Serverless VPC Access connector.
